contra.detail: Wunum's four-page Organised Phonology Data sheet gives one sentence on stress: 'In three syllable words or compound words the primary stress is on the penultimate syllable and the secondary stress on the first syllable.' (p. The penultimate primary agrees with Hatfield 2016 (p. 72: 'Stress in single words almost always falls on the penultimate syllable'). The secondary stress on the first syllable of simplex three-syllable words is not in Hatfield, whose only mention of secondary stress is for two-word compounds (pp. 72-73); for single words Hatfield states penultimate primary stress with a tendency to final stress under a complex coda (p. 72) and a shift to the ultima in lists or when call…

4234.prule: Penultimate stress in single (non-compound) words, 'almost always'; but a final syllable with a complex (two-consonant) coda tends to take the primary stress instead ([ku.ˈtɛmr] 'he cut'). Stress = higher impressionistic intensity, no vowel reduction. Two-syllable words with [h]/[ʔ] (kaha 'bad') stress the syllable after the [h]/[ʔ], i.e. final.
4234.srule: Not mentioned for simple (non-compound) words in Hatfield 2016, sec. 3.8 'Stress', pp. 72-73 (simple words have at most three syllables). 4235.dq: Trato, nesta seção, do acento em palavras dissilábicas, trissilábicas e polissilábicas em Mehináku, bem como de processos de juntura morfológica que atraem o acento, mudando suas posições canônicas. (p. 152) [...] o acento é fixo nas palavras trissilábicas e polissilábicas em Mehináku, uma vez que há um esforço na língua para manter o acento na penúltima sílaba desse tipo de palavra. (p. 156)

4235.heavy: Hayes (1995) definition adopted p. 152: 'sílaba leve é constituída por apenas uma vogal; sílaba pesada é constituída por vogal + consoante ou por vogal + vogal, o que forma um ditongo ou uma vogal longa'. Applied only to CVV suffixes/enclitics: '{=nau}; {=tai}; {=pai} e outros com estrutura CVV [...] formam um núcleo complexo, sendo, portanto, compreendidos como sílabas pesadas, razão pela qual tendem a atrair o acento' (p. 156). Syllable structure is (C)V (p. 70), so codas do not arise. de Felipe 2018 SETA pp. 118-119 additionally treats a long vowel in the first syllable of a disyllable as heavy ('recai na penúltima sílaba, caso esta seja pesada. Estamos entendendo sílaba pesada, aqui, como aquela que contêm uma vogal longa'), an account the 2020 thesis drops.
4235.dflt: Penultimate syllable in words of three or more syllables ('recai sempre na penúltima sílaba', p. 153); disyllables have no fixed position (lexically final or penult, exx. 107-108).
4235.prule: Default penultimate stress in words of three or more syllables (a.ˈmɨ.ɲa 'cold', ka.tu.pa.ˈlu.lu 'widow'); a final heavy CVV syllable supplied by a suffix/enclitic (=nau PL, =tai DIM, =pai IPFV) is treated as heavy and takes the stress (tɨneʐu=ˈnau 'women', ʂepi=ˈtsãĩ 'little bench', n=ãĩtʃa=ˈpai 'I am eating'); CV.CV suffixes keep the penult (itsa-ˈtɨpe 'canoes'). Disyllables have no fixed position: lexically final (pa.ˈpa 'father', ʂe.ˈpi 'bench') or penult (ˈu.nɨ 'water', ˈte.me 'tapir'). Monosyllabic VV/CVV words bear prominence on the first vowel (falling diphthong).

4237.tone: Tesfu 2003: 'Tone has morphological significance in the language' (p. 17) / 'Tone has grammatical significance in Malo' (p. 43): passive nominals derive from gerundives by HL > LL (gaco, pito, solo pairs); key (p. v) lists 'high tone' and 'low tone' diacritics but the glyphs did not print in the PDF, so the example pairs carry no visible marks; the words stress/accent/pitch/prominence do not occur anywhere in the thesis (a full-text search of the thesis). Azeb Amha 2007 (Encyclopaedia Aethiopica 3: 710, based on Tesfu 2003 plus one 2006 interview): between identical-looking short subject and possessive pronouns 'there probably exists a tone/accent difference between the two (this question is not discussed in Mahider Tesfu 2003; the author's own data are insufficient to draw a conclusion)'. Azeb Amha 1996 (SAL 25(2): 112-113, read): Malo appears only in the Ometo genealogical tree; the chart '(2) Prosodic Systems Claimed for Some Omotic Languages' (Tone: Dizi, Bench; Tonal-accent: Zayse, Gamo; Accent: Aari; Tone & Stress: Koorete) has no Malo entry. Hirut Woldemariam 2004: 26 says the described Ometo relatives (Wolaitta, Zayse, Gamo, Haro) are tone-accent languages with one H per simple word, but makes no claim about Malo. So: tonal by the only primary; whether it is a classical tone system or a one-H-per-word tone-accent system like its North Ometo relatives is undescribed.

4242.dq: Fox has a number of patterns of stress and intonation (cf. Voorhis 1971:70-73). The most frequently heard are the normal, interrogative, and exclamative. In normal intonation (the affirmative of Voorhis) the primary stress and highest pitch fall on the second or the fourth syllable from the end of the word, the penult or the pre-antepenult. ... Isolated words, as in one-word utterances or in list…
4242.dloc: Section E 'Prosodic Features', p. 160 (saved p. 4; read); intonation alternants pp. 160-162; Section F 'Clitics' pp. 163-166.
4242.prule: Normal (affirmative) intonation, word inside an ordinary sentence: primary stress, coinciding with highest pitch, on the pre-antepenult (4th syllable from the end) in words of four or more syllables, and on the penult in words of two or three syllables; equivalently, discounting the devoiced final vowel, on the third or first syllable from the end of the stressable syllables. Position counted from the right edge, no reference to syllable weight.
4242.srule: Occasional, not rhythmic: Goddard marks secondary stress (grave) where recorded and notes that in normal intonation 'one sometimes hears unexpected primary or secondary penultimate stress' (ex. 9 nemečíme·nèmo̥: primary on the pre-antepenult, secondary on the penult); under exclamative intonation (main stress on the final vowel) there is 'a more or less distinct secondary stress on the pre-antepenult', never on the penult. No regular secondary-stress rule is given.

4251.heavy: (Jacobi's position only) syllable quantity in the metrical sense: 'von der Prosodie des Wortes... bestimmt', 'durch die Quantität bestimmten', 'mit kurzer Pänultima... denen mit langer und darum nebentoniger'; heaviness is not defined in the section (Latin-type by his comparison; Bloch reports Jacobi's rule as 'on the first long vowel starting from the end of the word').
4251.prule: No rule of record: the reachable primaries disagree on the locus. Jacobi 1921: word accent placed mechanically by syllable quantity as in Latin (Prakrit), with in Apabhramsa a competing 'organic' accent on the stem syllable (verb root; disyllabic nominal stems), the language preferring endings with a light penult to avoid a second accent. Pischel 1900 sec. 46: the accent of poetic Apabhramsa 'entspricht wesentlich dem vedischen' (lexically fixed Vedic place), predominantly expiratory. Tagare 1948: accent on the initial syllable; 'the penultimate syllable was definitely unaccented in EAp.' Bloch 1965: Middle Indian furnishes no decisive facts for a regular stress accent; Pischel's and Jacobi's evidence 'open to other explanations, especially rhythm'.
4251.srule: Jacobi 1921 only, hedged reconstruction: where the main accent sits on the stem syllable, a long penult would carry a quantity-determined 'Nebenton' (secondary accent), e.g. paṇavānta (stem accent on paṇ-, Nebenton on -ān-); endings with a long, 'therefore secondarily accented', penult are disfavoured, the language tending to level such double accentuation. No rhythmic/iterative secondary stress described. Pischel 1900 sec. 46, Tagare 1948 and Bloch 1965 say nothing about secondary stress.

4255.prule: No positional rule. The only specialist treatment of Luwic accent (Billing 2023/2026, covering 'Lycian' = Lycian A and Lycian B/Milyan as two dialects) characterises the Lycian word accent as a stress accent (not pitch or tone) that is 'free, or non-demarcative' ('All languages have free accent'), largely columnar within paradigms with some possible mobility, and recoverable only negatively: a syncopated vowel or a syllabic resonant (m̃, ñ) was unaccented, since the Lycian alphabet does not mark accent. Milyan (Lycian B) forms are among the evidence: trpplẽ 'threefold' < *tri-plóm (final-syllable accent, initial syncope), mrssxa- 'defilement' < *m(V)rs-aH-á- (oxytone a-stem), trppala-/mutala-/xumala-/ziwala-/rm̃pala- (agent nouns in -ala- assigned penultimate accent -ála-); i.e. within Lycian B a-stems the accent falls on different syllables in words of the same shape, which is position fixed per lexeme/formation, not by counting from an edge or by weight.

4258.tone: The source's topic is incipient tonogenesis: the default final accent is realized by pitch (raised F0 / rising-high melody, phonetic tone numbers given) rather than intensity; 'Stress is not contrastive in Mongolic, including in SEM'; tone is non-distinctive in most environments but a small set of otherwise homophonous pairs contrasts final high vs penult prominence + final falling pitch: bosi 'cloth' vs 'louse', dasi 'we' vs 'thread', chige 'ear' vs 'to see', wulang 'drinking' vs 'many'. Utterance-final syllables show downdrift instead of the raised melody. Chinese loans take the default low-high (final) pattern regardless of original Chinese tone (jiaozi, contra Li 1986 for Baonan). Conclusion: 'an incipient tonal or at least pitch accent system', but 'the underlying patterning is still one of prominence assignment to final syllables'.

4260.exq_: No exceptions mentioned. The parenthetical is the paper's only stress rule; its one other use of 'unstressed' ('clusters were reduced to a nasal when preceded by an unstressed syllable') is a sound-change statement, not an exception.
4260.sec_quote: This is a trait shared by all Karnic languages and results from a very early (common Kamic) sound change in which homorganic nasal+stop clusters were reduced to a nasal when preceded by an unstressed syllable.
